meta.title: Who really said "In the future everyone will be world-famous for 15 minutes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The line first appeared in Warhol's 1968 Stockholm catalogue — inserted by curator Pontus Hulten, who could not find it in any Warhol material.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In the future everyone will be world-famous for 15 minutes'?
meta.ogDescription: Warhol's most famous line went into his 1968 Moderna Museet catalogue on a curator's say-so: 'If he didn't say it, he could very well have said it.'

answer.label: Attributed to Andy Warhol — but the source is disputed
answer.sourceLine: The famous wording first reached print in the book produced for Warhol’s February–March 1968 retrospective at Moderna Museet in Stockholm, as “In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes.” The museum’s own published account, written by Olle Granath — the man who compiled that book’s selection of Warhol quotations — says the line was nowhere in the box of Warhol material he had been given, and that curator Pontus Hultén told him to include it anyway. A looser version had already been reported as Warhol’s in Time in October 1967, and Warhol used and rewrote the line for years afterwards, so the idea was circulating as his; the exact sentence is not documented anywhere in his own words.

source.excerpt: In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes.
trail: The earliest evidence Quote Investigator located for any version is Time of 13 October 1967, which reports Warhol predicting the day “when everyone will be famous for 15 minutes” — unsourced, and without the word “world,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

The polished wording appears in the catalogue of Warhol’s Stockholm exhibition of 1968, which is the source Wikiquote ↗ gives for the line; Moderna Museet’s own shop lists the 1968 poster under the wording “In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes ↗.”

Olle Granath, who compiled the book’s quotations, writes that the line was not in the material he was given and that Pontus Hultén had it inserted regardless — an account published by Moderna Museet ↗ and quoted in full by Word Histories ↗.

Warhol’s biographer Blake Gopnik collects the competing claims — Hultén, Nat Finkelstein, Larry Rivers, Billy Al Bengston, Billy Name — and a 1980 cable interview in which Warhol himself is asked about having said he never uttered the line, on Warholiana ↗; Smithsonian ↗ summarises the case.
source.excerptNote: Moderna Museet describes the 1968 book as having four parts, one of them a small selection of quotations and aphorisms attributed to Warhol; the line appeared there, and was then set in large type on a series of about ten exhibition posters in place of the usual reproduction of a painting. Note the difference from the version people quote today: the 1968 printing has “everybody,” unhyphenated “world famous” and “fifteen minutes.”

source.rightsNote: The sentence’s first known publication is the book and poster series made for Warhol’s 1968 Moderna Museet retrospective — far too recent for the United States public domain, so treat the text as in copyright. Moderna Museet’s own reproduction of that 1968 poster carries the notice “©/®/TM The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts Inc. / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.” Rights are a separate question from attribution: who actually composed the sentence remains disputed.

author.name: Andy Warhol
author.heading: About Andy Warhol
author.metaLine: 1928–1987 · American Pop artist, filmmaker and magazine publisher
author.bio: Andy Warhol (born Andrew Warhola Jr. in Pittsburgh) was the central figure of American Pop art, turning soup cans, Brillo boxes and Marilyn Monroe into silkscreened icons and running the Manhattan studio known as the Factory. His work was largely about fame — how mass media manufactures it, multiplies it and throws it away — which is exactly why the “fifteen minutes” line fits him so perfectly that almost nobody has ever checked it. Warhol was also, by his own cheerful admission, a magpie for other people’s lines, and he spent the late 1970s deliberately garbling this one.

Authorship of the 1968 wording is disputed: Olle Granath, who compiled the book’s quotations, records that it was inserted at curator Pontus Hultén’s instruction.

misattribution.heading: Five people have been named as the source
misattribution.intro: “Fifteen minutes of fame” is Warhol’s most quoted line and his least documented one. Several people have claimed it or been credited with it, and the popular wording is not even the wording that was printed.

items.why: Olle Granath, who read the whole box of Warhol material and compiled the book’s quotations, says the line was not in it. Hultén told him to add it anyway: “If he didn’t say it, he could very well have said it.” The account is published by Moderna Museet itself ↗.

In a 2005 account Finkelstein said that during a shoot he told Warhol that everybody wants to be famous “for about 15 minutes.” But in his own 1989 book he had credited the words to Warhol and mentioned no theft, as Blake Gopnik notes ↗.

George Rickey’s Constructivism: Origins and Evolution, with a preface dated July 1967, has “as Larry Rivers says, ‘Everybody will be famous’” — the idea without the time limit, and Rivers was a Warhol insider, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The popular form runs “everyone … world-famous … 15 minutes”; the 1968 printing reads “everybody … world famous … fifteen minutes.” The versions Warhol demonstrably wrote himself drop “world” altogether — his diary of 27 July 1978 and Andy Warhol’s Exposures (1979), where he says he is bored with the line, both per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No manuscript, recording or interview in Warhol’s own words has ever been produced containing this sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ still credits Warhol with more than one version of the saying — the 1968 catalogue line and the one in his 1978 diary — while stressing that the phrasing was always highly variable and that Warhol kept deliberately altering it.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Warhol anyway
lead: Warhol spent his career making art about manufactured celebrity, so a one-sentence prophecy about disposable fame was always going to be shelved under his name. What makes the case genuinely Warholian is that his single most quoted line may itself be a piece of mass-produced attribution — printed, repeated and believed until it became true, which is more or less the argument the line is making.

The trail is unusually well documented for a contested quote. Time reported a version in October 1967 without saying where it came from; the polished sentence appeared in Stockholm four months later; and by the mid-1970s it was loose in the culture, quoted by Dustin Hoffman and others as common property, according to Warhol biographer Blake Gopnik ↗. Warhol himself grew bored of it and started rewriting it: “In fifteen minutes everybody will be famous.”
context.detailsSummary: How the line got into the Stockholm book
detailsBody: Pontus Hultén, then director of Moderna Museet, handed Olle Granath a box said to contain everything written by and about Warhol and asked him to build the book’s text section from it. Granath read the lot, delivered a manuscript, and Hultén rang back to say one quotation was missing — the fifteen-minutes line. Granath replied that if it had been in the material he would have spotted it. Hultén’s answer, as Granath recalls it on the museum’s own website ↗: “If he didn’t say it, he could very well have said it.” In it went.

The book’s quotations were then set in large type on a series of about ten exhibition posters instead of the usual reproduction of a painting — which is how the sentence, rather than any single painting, became the visual signature of the show. Moderna Museet still sells a reproduction of that 1968 poster ↗, carrying the wording “In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes.”

One first-hand account cuts the other way. In a 2008 interview quoted by Blake Gopnik, the Factory photographer Billy Name said Warhol produced the line himself while the group was sitting around planning the Stockholm catalogue — “so it went in the catalogue.” Nobody has been able to reconcile the two recollections.
context.pull: The line that defined Warhol is the one thing about him nobody can source.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest evidence QI located is Time of 13 October 1967, reporting Warhol predicting the day "when everyone will be famous for 15 minutes"; the 1968 Moderna Museet catalogue carried "In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes"; Rickey's 1967 Constructivism credits Larry Rivers with "Everybody will be famous"; Warhol's 27 July 1978 diary entry and Andy Warhol's Exposures (1979) contain versions without "world"; QI concludes Warhol is properly credited with more than one version.

Olle Granath's first-person account, published by Moderna Museet, states that Pontus Hulten gave him a box of everything written by and about Warhol, that the fifteen-minutes quotation was not in it, and that Hulten said "If he didn't say it, he could very well have said it. Let's put it in." It also describes the book's quotations being used on about ten exhibition posters instead of a reproduction of a painting.

Moderna Museet's shop sells a reproduction of the 1968 poster titled "In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes," describes the 1968 catalogue as having four parts including a small selection of Warhol quotes and aphorisms, retells Granath's exchange with Hulten, and carries the notice "©/®/TM The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts Inc. 2014/ Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York."

Blake Gopnik documents that Granath found no trace of the line, that Hulten said "If he didn't say it, he very well could have. Let's put it in," plus rival claims by Nat Finkelstein (2005 account of a 1965 shoot, contradicted by his own 1989 book), Larry Rivers via Rickey 1967, Philip Pearlstein, Billy Al Bengston, and Billy Name's 2008 account that Warhol said it while planning the Stockholm catalogue; also a 1980 cable interview in which Warhol is asked about having said he never uttered it.

Wikiquote lists "In the future everyone will be world-famous for 15 minutes" in its main sourced Andy Warhol quotations, sourced to the catalogue of an exhibition of his art in Stockholm, Sweden (1968), notes common paraphrases, and separately quotes Andy Warhol's Exposures (1979) on Studio 54 with the version omitting "world."

Smithsonian Magazine reports that Warhol probably never said the line, that Blake Gopnik traces it to a 1968 Swedish exhibition publication and suggests Pontus Hulten coined it, and that other claimants include Larry Rivers and Nat Finkelstein, who said he replied "Yeah, for about 15 minutes, Andy."

Word Histories quotes Olle Granath's account of the Hulten exchange in full, gives the 1968 Moderna Museet wording as "In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes," and documents a 1973 Guardian use of "famous for 15 minutes" with no reference to Warhol.

Andy Warhol was born Andrew Warhola Jr. on 6 August 1928 in Pittsburgh and died 22 February 1987; he is an American artist and filmmaker credited with popularizing the expression "15 minutes of fame."
